extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of comedy, literary critics, humorists, and authors studying comic theory
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of comic techniques in writing
extracted.subtask_description: The page is a theoretical/literary analysis of how the comic operates in words and character, describing mechanisms (transposition, exaggeration, automatism, gesture vs action) that produce laughter and how to deploy or recognize them in writing and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition between solemn and familiar (parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transpose the solemn into the familiar and the result is parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The effect is produced when an idea normally expressed in a lofty key is rendered in familiar terms (example: Jean Paul Richter's dawn compared to a lobster being boiled). The reverse transposition (familiar into solemn) yields an opposite comic current; both directions are main sources of comic fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation as one form of transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic can appear as degradation: making something that was formerly dignified appear mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers who define the comic as degradation capture only one form of the broader transposition principle; degradation is not the sole source of laughter—transposition has many other manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (systematic/prolonged)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of small things as though they were large is to exaggerate; exaggeration is always comic when prolonged and especially when systematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic exaggeration can produce powerful comic effects (e.g., mock-heroic poems); habitual braggadocio often becomes comic through its mock-heroic aspect. Exaggeration is a striking but limited subset of comic transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward transposition of moral value (respectable language for disreputable things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing a disreputable idea or low-class behaviour in the utmost 'respectability' is generally comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice — common in English literature (Dickens, Thackeray) — can be effective in a word or brief phrase if it reveals an entire system of transposition accepted in certain social circles (example: Gogol's 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast real vs ideal: irony versus humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition between what is (real) and what ought to be (ideal) can produce irony or humour: stating what ought to be and pretending it's what is gives irony; describing what is and pretending it's what ought to be gives humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is oratorical and can become high-pressure eloquence; humour is scientific, delights in concrete terms and technical details, and is the counterpart of irony. Both are forms of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional/jargon transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into a profession's technical vocabulary creates comic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying business or professional phraseology to social relations (e.g., treating marriage as a business affair in Labiche) produces laughter and may disclose a fault in character when it reveals a commercial mindset applied to sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language's mechanical/ready-made elements produce comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Language attains laughable results because it is a human product containing ready-made, stereotyped, mechanical elements that can be transposed or inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If language were wholly supple and perfectly unified, it would evade the comic. The rigid, the ready-made, the mechanical — in contrast with the living and ever-changing — are defects laughter singles out and would correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social corrective (comic's social meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter has a social meaning: it expresses a lack of adaptability to society and functions as a kind of social 'ragging' to humiliate or correct the unsociable individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy belongs neither wholly to art nor to life; even on stage laughter carries an unconscious intent to humiliate/correct. The comic reproves absentmindedness or rigidity that resists social fitting-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsociability / rigidity as source of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual who automatically goes his own way without adapting to fellow beings (unsociable/rigid) is comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigidity — withdrawing into one's own personality or habits — causes the person to be subject to ridicule because comedy largely arises from such withdrawal. A rigid virtue can be more comic than a flexible vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic depends on lack of emotional sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter appeals to intelligence and is incompatible with emotion; to be comic a situation or fault must not arouse sympathy, fear, or pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If depiction arouses feeling, it prevents laughter. Even serious vices can be made ludicrous only when arranged so they leave our emotions unaffected. Preventing emotional contagion is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to prevent sympathy (isolation of feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic poet prevents sympathy by isolating the feeling within the character, making it a parasitic, rigid element that fails to connect with the rest of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An emotion that is rigid and isolated shows puppet-like movements and alienates spectator sympathy (example: Harpagon's greed passing by other feelings without affecting them). This art of 'throwing a wet blanket upon sympathy' is used unconsciously by comic writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gesture rather than action
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy directs attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, language as automatic expressions) rather than to action (intentional, consequential behaviour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesture is automatic, an isolated part of the person, often slipping out unawares; action is intentional and engages the whole person. When attention is fixed on gesture, matters are prevented from being taken seriously and the realm of comedy is entered (example: Tartuffe's humanitarian gestures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / involuntary expression as essence of laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically: involuntary gestures, unconscious remarks, absentmindedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deeper the absentmindedness the higher the comedy (systematic absentmindedness, as in Don Quixote, being supremely comic). Comic characters must unwittingly betray aspects of themselves; self-inattention makes them laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions and self-exposure in comic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic characters often contradict their stated principles by immediately exhibiting the condemned behaviour (e.g., inveighing against anger then flying into a passion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contradictions expose the character's obliviousness to self and help the audience locate the obviousness that produces laughter; they function as practical devices to reveal automatism and inattention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type/stock-character and generality as comic aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Every comic character is a type; comedy aims at depicting general types rather than unique, individuated persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy seeks the generality — ready-made elements of personality — so that characters crystallise into categories others may fall into. High-class comedy depicts general types; this generality distinguishes comedy from tragedy/drama, which weld characters to particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic proportional to rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect is proportioned to the rigidity of the character or element being depicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving aside what moves our sensibility, all the rest of personality can become comic, and the degree of comedy increases with how mechanised or clockwork-like (rigid, ready-made) that trait is.
